papers.title: DynaMimic: A Physics-Informed World Model for Humanoid Motion Tracking
papers.abstract: Whole-body motion tracking enables humanoid robots to reproduce diverse skills from human demonstrations. Existing model-free reinforcement learning methods either distill motion specialists into a single policy at the cost of performance or train a generalist policy directly using cluster-scale computation. SuperMimic reduces this computational cost through a differentiable world model that implicitly learns the physics shared across motions by predicting the next state from the current state and action. However, this implicit formulation may not fully capture the underlying physical processes. Errors around changes of support can accumulate over imagined rollouts used to train the tracking policy. To address this challenge, we introduce DynaMimic, a differentiable world model that explicitly incorporates shared physics into state prediction. Specifically, its network predicts a contact wrench at each candidate support link and a residual generalized force. DynaMimic then uses these predictions to compute the next state through closed-form Lagrangian forward dynamics. Across 60 full LAFAN1 motions, DynaMimic reduces mean per-joint position error (MPJPE) by 18.6% relative to SuperMimic. For terrain tracking, we give both methods the same local height maps. Relative to terrain-conditioned SuperMimic, DynaMimic reduces MPJPE by 14.9% on A3 Parkour (66.15 to 56.28~mm) and by 10.8% on GRAIL terrain clips (141.88 to 126.57~mm). On a real A3 humanoid, the learned policies can perform diverse skills, such as floor recovery, cartwheel and a box vault.

papers.title: Atomic Policy: Composing Atomic Manipulation Skills with Agentic Reasoning
papers.abstract: Long-horizon manipulation requires robots to translate task intent into physical interactions as the scene changes. Vision-language models (VLMs) offer semantic and spatial reasoning, while visuomotor policies provide fine-grained control. Yet ambiguous goals and dependencies between actions make their integration challenging. We introduce Atomic Policy, a framework that composes learned manipulation skills through grounded steering and execution feedback. A VLM estimates the symbolic state and goal, and a PDDL solver constructs a skill plan. An agentic harness steers each skill through language, visual pointing, or both, and verifies its outcome to guide phase transitions and replanning. A common phase-level interface supports specialized policies and generalist action models. Experiments in simulation and on a real robot show how Atomic Policy improves task following and supports recovery in complex, long-horizon manipulation. Project page: https://aaronzkd.github.io/atomic-policy/

papers.title: Simulator-as-Proxy World Model for Robot Manipulation
papers.abstract: Video world models for robots are increasingly conditioned on a simulated or rendered proxy of the scene, on the assumption that the video will show what the proxy shows. Testing this assumption requires a proxy whose state is explicit and can be perturbed. We present SimPWM (Simulator-as-Proxy World Model): given a calibrated camera, it represents, from the first frame alone, the robot by its 3D model and the objects the gripper may touch as 3D points; a rule-based simulator with no trained parameters moves them under the actions, and a video model renders the result. SimPWM returns the realistic video together with the simulated state. We then freeze the simulated objects while the arm moves as recorded and check whether the video still shows the object lifted. On DROID episodes from unseen setups, the answer differs for the arm and for the objects. With each of three base video models, the arm follows the proxy (robot IoU 0.75-0.78, against at most 0.69 for end-to-end models); rendering the robot alone already gives this. What the simulated objects add is the object state: against a robot-only proxy, they cut missed pick-ups from 54% to 38%, and the video follows them only with some base models: on rigid objects, freezing them lowers the lift rate of MiniMax-H3, fine-tuned on episodes whose simulation agrees with the real video, from 42% to 10%, but that of LTX-2.3, trained on the same episodes, only from 57% to 49%, as if it inferred the grasp from the arm motion; more than half of the remaining lifts of MiniMax-H3 are of cloth and rope, which the simulator carries rigidly. With any base model, the simulated state records what the simulation did; under perturbed actions, a video that disagrees with it reveals that the video ignores the simulated state.

papers.title: Embodied AI Fails the Mirror Test: How a Simple Mirror Breaks Robot Policies
papers.abstract: Can a simple mirror expose the limitations of today's robotic manipulation policies? Inspired by the mirror self-recognition test in animal cognition, we investigate whether robot policies can reliably manipulate physical objects in scenes containing their reflections. We introduce RoboDojo-Mirror, a benchmark built on RoboDojo that preserves task objectives, success criteria, and policy checkpoints while comparing a mirror-free baseline with single-mirror, dual-mirror, and mirrored-tabletop conditions. Across five policies spanning Vision-Language-Action models, World Action Models, and agentic policies, every mirror condition reduces aggregate success rates: averaged over the three conditions, the drop ranges from 10.8 to 56.7 percentage points across policies, and it reaches 62.5 points on the mirrored tabletop. Because a mirror is also a physical obstacle, we compare it against geometrically matched non-reflective panels; 50--88\% of mirror-specific failures occur without recorded robot--panel contact, so direct collisions alone do not explain the degradation. Trajectory and contact analyses instead reveal recurring behaviors consistent with phantom targeting of reflected objects and spatial mislocalization of real ones. Targeted diagnostics further characterize grasping near reflections, policy-dependent pushing progress, and physical-target interaction under main-camera occlusion. Real-robot experiments with $π_{0.5}$ and FastWAM also show lower overall success rates under the upright-mirror and mirrored-tabletop conditions. These findings reveal a shared vulnerability to reflective environments across diverse robot policies and motivate reflection-aware evaluation of embodied intelligence. Code is available at https://github.com/iPPLab/robodojo-mirror.

papers.title: CAPER: PartGround and PlanRefine for Reliable Manual-Guided Robotic Assembly Planning
papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Models (VLMs) used in robot task planning to derive assembly procedures from existing manuals may correctly interpret individual assembly actions yet confuse exact part identities, predict unsupported Part IDs, or produce inconsistent parts across assembly steps. Thus, we propose CAPER (Capacity-Aware Part-grounding and Evidence Refinement), a manual-guided robotic assembly framework that enables VLMs to generate assembly procedures with two modules--PartGround and PlanRefine. PartGround aligns step-level manual evidence with product-specific inventory and part-reference information to identify exact Part IDs and quantities, transforming free-form hardware prediction into evidence-guided assignments represented in a shared Assembly Intermediate Representation (Assembly IR). PlanRefine audits PartGround assignments against finite inventory by removing the lowest-confidence assignments. Uncertain identity cases remain marked for review in the Assembly IR. We evaluate CAPER on the IKEA Assembly in the Wild (IAW) dataset. Experiment results show that CAPER reaches a Finite-inventory Consistency Rate of 83.33% and produces zero observed out-of-inventory Part-ID occurrences. At the plan level, PlanRefine removes all observed inventory-overuse pairs (9 -> 0) and excess units (51 -> 0). Overall, the results indicate that PartGround and PlanRefine improve part reliability, while also enhancing finite-inventory consistency and local prediction accuracy. Project page and video: https://xhzzzz123.github.io/CAPER/

papers.title: Keypose or Dense? A Controlled Comparison of Action Representations for Stage-Structured Manipulation
papers.abstract: Most imitation policies that predict chunks of future actions use the dense action representation, in which the chunk holds one control target per step. In stage-structured manipulation, where a task can be divided into stages with definable endpoints, the keypose action representation instead sets each step of the chunk to the endpoint of the stage that step belongs to, and a speed-capped servo supplies the motion. We compare the two in several simulated manipulation tasks and on a real robot, with the same chunk length and matched demonstrations, observations, policy architectures and update budgets; in simulation, each one's execution rule is selected on tuning scenes. When the simulated demonstrations are slowed, paused and rerouted, dense success falls sharply while keypose stays roughly level, across three policy architectures and with endpoints extracted from the recorded demonstrations; keypose also leads under object-size and position shift. With clean demonstrations, keypose leads only when they are scarce and is otherwise close to or behind dense across the simulated tasks, provided that the demonstrations and execution rule suit its executor; when they do not, it falls far below dense. The same dependence on the executor appeared on a real robot learning to open a drawer from human demonstrations: dense succeeded more often, and keypose improved substantially only after its executor's rotation and forward speed were adjusted to the demonstrations. These results suggest that keypose trades sensitivity to such variation in the demonstrations for sensitivity to execution that departs from them.

papers.title: Uncertainty Quantification and Global Sensitivity Analysis of Patient-Specific Coronary Hemodynamics Under Unsteady Flow Conditions
papers.abstract: Patient-specific computational models of the coronary arteries demonstrate transformative potential for physiological assessment, identifying hemodynamic markers associated with disease progression, and optimizing treatment. Unfortunately, these models rarely account for input parameter uncertainty, limiting confidence in predictions and their clinical interpretation. Herein, we present a novel uncertainty quantification-finite element framework that integrates computationally efficient techniques to characterize and propagate uncertainty through patient-specific coronary simulations under unsteady flow conditions. Principal component analysis characterized variability in pulsatile coronary velocity waveforms, while uncertainty in blood pressure, viscosity, density, and heart rate is represented through probability distributions. Polynomial chaos expansion (PCE) enabled efficient uncertainty propagation and global sensitivity analysis across three patient-specific models, quantifying variability in time-averaged wall shear stress (WSS), oscillatory shear index, and cross-flow index. Fourth-order PCE emulators converged across all three patients, yielding analyses of 505 models per patient, with median coefficients of variation ranging from 0.15-0.20 for time-averaged WSS, 0.54-0.75 for oscillatory shear index, and 0.28-0.38 for cross-flow index, highlighting greater relative uncertainty in multidirectional WSS metrics. Global sensitivity analysis revealed that time-averaged WSS variability was governed by the individual effects of velocity and blood viscosity, with parameter interactions contributing <2% of total variance. In contrast, velocity waveform uncertainty dominated variability in the oscillatory shear index and cross-flow index, with higher-order parameter interactions accounting for 20.7-34.5% and 26.6-37.8% of total variance, respectively.

papers.title: High-Receiver-Bandwidth MRI Near Metal Implants with Motion-Consistent Rep2Rep Denoising
papers.abstract: Purpose: To develop and evaluate a self-supervised denoising approach using motion-consistent Rep2Rep learning to enable high-receiver-bandwidth MRI for reduced metal-induced distortion. Methods: Motion-consistent Rep2Rep generates anatomically consistent training repetitions in the presence of inter-repetition motion by combining two acquired repetitions and splitting the combined k-space along the readout direction. The model was trained on 134 clinical low-receiver-bandwidth (300 Hz/pixel) MRI datasets and applied to 59 high-receiver-bandwidth (1028 Hz/pixel) MRI datasets. Three musculoskeletal radiologists independently scored low- and high-receiver-bandwidth images (before and after denoising) in a blinded manner for metal artifact reduction, image sharpness, perceived SNR, and overall image quality. A separate blinded reader preference evaluation was performed to compare motion-consistent Rep2Rep with standard Rep2Rep. Results: High-receiver-bandwidth MRI significantly reduced metal-induced artifact, while motion-consistent Rep2Rep improved perceived SNR and overall image quality. Compared to clinical low-receiver-bandwidth MRI, denoised high-receiver-bandwidth MRI achieved significantly higher metal artifact reduction scores (sagittal: 3.69 vs 3.01; axial: 3.83 vs 3.05; both P<0.0001) and comparable overall image quality scores (sagittal: 4.03 vs 3.98, P = 0.5391; axial: 3.95 vs 3.87, P=0.1266). The high-receiver-bandwidth axial protocol also reduced acquisition time by 47%. Motion-consistent Rep2Rep better preserved fine anatomical details than standard Rep2Rep. Conclusion: High-receiver-bandwidth MRI with motion-consistent self-supervised Rep2Rep denoising reduces metal-induced artifact without requiring dedicated high-receiver-bandwidth training data. This offers a practical approach for MRI near metal implants, such as postoperative cervical spine imaging.

papers.title: Excess noise and electron-phonon energy transfer in Au wires: Length and temperature effects
papers.abstract: As a mesoscopic diffusive wire at low temperatures is driven out of equilibrium by a current, excess noise is observed compared to the equilibrium Johnson-Nyquist fluctuations. The expected form of the excess noise varies depending on the relative rates of wire traversal, electron-electron inelastic energy transfer, and electron-phonon inelastic energy transfer. We measure noise as a function of bias current in diffusive Au nanowires on SiO2/Si with lengths ranging from sub-μm to 30 μm and temperatures from 3 K to 50 K, to map out the interplay between charge shot noise and the crossover to electron self-heating and phonon-dominated noise suppression. As expected qualitatively, shot noise is suppressed with increasing wire length and substrate temperature, as electron-phonon scattering is of increasing importance. In long wires, the simple model of electron-phonon energy loss known to be quantitatively effective below a few Kelvin underpredicts the excess noise in the high bias, high temperature limit. This issue is more severe in wires on SiO2/Si than on bare Si, implying that interfacial thermal conduction must be considered in the thermal path even at comparatively high temperatures.

papers.title: Interface and film engineering for improved spin-charge interconversion in sputtered GeTe nanodevices
papers.abstract: Spin-logic devices promise non-volatile logic-in-memory computing with ultra-low power consumption, offering a route to circumvent the von Neumann bottleneck. Magnetoelectric and ferroelectric spin-orbit (MESO/FESO) devices, however, require spin-charge interconversion materials that combine a large output signal with properties that survive nanoscale integration. Tellurides are particularly fragile in this respect, as processing readily introduces defects that degrade their spin-charge interconversion properties. Here we demonstrate room-temperature spin-charge interconversion in patterned FESO nanoscale devices based on sputtered GeTe, with feature sizes down to 100 nm. By introducing a Ti interfacial layer between the CoFe electrode and GeTe, and by using GeTe films of improved crystalline quality, we increase the interconversion output signal from 3 mΩ to 24 mΩ, exceeding values reported for platinum at comparable device size. These results establish large-scale-deposited GeTe as a viable material platform for spin-logic devices and identify interface quality and film crystallinity as key levers for optimizing their performance.

papers.title: Molecular Pawns on a Surface Chessboard: Computational Investigation of Nanographenes with Atomistic Methods
papers.abstract: Atomically precise nanographenes combine tunable electronic topology with localized, coherent spin states, making them candidate platforms for molecular quantum technologies. This review examines the multiscale theoretical framework governing these systems: the hierarchy of computational methods for describing magnetic properties, the substrate-molecule interface, on-surface synthetic kinetics, and supramolecular self-assembly. We highlight how density functional theory, automated reaction-path discovery, and spin-aware machine-learned interatomic potentials connect static electronic structure to mesoscale dynamics, and how magnetic exchange, optical excitations, and spin transport can be predicted before synthesis.

papers.title: Dirac-like bands and weak-field transverse transport in ABA trilayer graphene
papers.abstract: The low-energy electronic structure of ABA trilayer graphene is composed of light and heavy electron branches, which can be altered by an out-of-plane displacement field. Here, we show that, depending on the values of Slonczewski-Weiss-McClure parameters, a displacement field can inflict a band edge inversion, for which we identify the inversion conditions. This inversion is accompanied by a reversal of Berry curvature and giant topological magnetic moments at the band edges. In a weak perpendicular magnetic field, those topological magnetic moments produce valley splitting, giving rise to distinct anomalous transverse electrical and thermoelectric responses. These features offer a potential route to detecting the band inversion and constraining several of the least established tight-binding parameters, such as the on-site energy shift for the dimer pair of carbons $Δ^\prime$ and the next neighbour hopping parameters $γ_2$ and $γ_5$.

papers.title: Towards determination of intrinsic spin properties in MAPbI$_3$ crystals using spin noise spectroscopy
papers.abstract: Spin noise spectroscopy in back- and forward-scattering geometries is used to study the spin dynamics of charge carriers in a MAPbI$_3$ (MA = methylammonium) single crystal. The spectra reveal electrons and holes with different degrees of localization. At low temperatures ($T \approx 4$~K), hole spin relaxation is dominated by the hyperfine interaction with nuclear spins. The broadening of the spectra with increasing temperature can be attributed to thermally activated hopping of localized holes. From the thermal activation energies, we estimate hole localization lengths that are consistent with both the hyperfine-induced dephasing rates and the zero-field frequency shifts measured at low temperature. By contrast, the electron spin dynamics cannot be explained by the hyperfine interaction alone: even at the lowest excitation powers, it is affected by the probe light, and we observe a slowing down of spin relaxation with increasing power. Comparison of the back- and forward-scattered spin noise signals indicates that the spatial distribution of carriers is inhomogeneous: electrons are located preferentially near the crystal surface, weakly localized holes (characterized by slower spin relaxation) are found mostly away from the surface, and strongly localized holes are somewhere in between.

papers.title: LeIFF: A localized-electron and ion force field for coupled nuclear and electronic dynamics
papers.abstract: Classical and machine-learned interatomic potentials enable large-scale simulations by replacing electronic structure with an effective energy surface for nuclear motion. This excludes electronic dynamics, electronic excitation and energy exchange between electrons and ions. First-principles electron dynamics can describe these processes, but its computational cost restricts system sizes and simulation times. Electron force fields offer an intermediate description by treating electrons as semiclassical dynamical particles interacting with ions. We introduce the localized-electron and ion force field (LeIFF), a compact physical model for both ground state bonding and excited electron dynamics. Valence electrons are represented by spin-labeled spherical charge distributions with dynamical centers and widths. The energy combines analytic electronic kinetic, Coulomb, and dispersion terms with spline-interpolated short-range interactions fitted to a large molecular data set. The resulting energy surface describes a variety of ground state properties across diverse bonding environments and charge states. It also provides a qualitative description of electronic behavior away from equilibrium. It shows improved robustness, accuracy, and transferability relative to earlier electron force-fields. Without any solid-state training, the same model describes dielectric screening and collective electronic response in silicon. LeIFF thus opens a route to large-scale simulations of nonadiabatic processes in molecules and solids, combining chemical bonding and nonequilibrium electronic motion within a common physical framework.

papers.title: Tunable first-order transitions and magnetic hysteresis in Bernal pentalayer graphene
papers.abstract: In two-dimensional electron systems, strong Coulomb interactions can spontaneously lift flavor degeneracies such as spin and valley, producing first-order transitions with hysteretic switching of interest for memory devices. The subband degree of freedom in multiband systems may be viewed as a flavor that not only participates in such transitions but also enables control of the hysteretic behavior, as a displacement field can shift the energy difference between subbands. Here, we demonstrate this principle in Bernal-stacked pentalayer graphene, whose low-energy spectrum comprises a monolayer-like Dirac sub-band together with light and heavy bilayer-like sub-bands. Local compressibility measurements resolve a fully symmetry-broken Landau-level spectrum and a sequence of phase transitions that occur when Landau levels of different subbands cross, at which strong interactions redistribute the occupation among flavors. We show that these transitions exhibit hysteretic Hall responses in magnetic field, confirming their first-order character, and that the magnitude and sign of the hysteresis are tuned by the displacement field, as expected from the subband Landau-level ordering determined in compressibility measurements. Our work establishes the subband degree of freedom in multiband systems as a resource for engineering hysteretic switching, and highlights how local thermodynamic measurements can link microscopic insights to macroscopic responses in quantum materials.

papers.title: Environmentally assisted transport in a diamond chain
papers.abstract: We study quantum transport in a diamond chain coupled to Markovian reservoirs at its boundaries. The system is subject to uniform dephasing and an external magnetic field threading a flux $Φ$ per plaquette. We derive exact analytical solutions for $Φ=0$ and $Φ=π$. We show that in the all-bands-flat regime at $Φ=π$, dephasing destroys Aharonov-Bohm caging, leading to environment-assisted quantum transport. Our results demonstrate that coupling a flat-band system to a dissipative environment provides a viable route for controlling transport in regimes where coherent dynamics alone would result in complete localization.

papers.title: CPU-Eval: Evaluating Large Language Models for CPU Hardware Code Generation
papers.abstract: Benchmarks such as VerilogEval have supported rapid advances in hardware description language (HDL) generation by large language models (LLMs). However, recent HDL-generation systems achieve pass rates above 90% on VerilogEval, leaving limited headroom for revealing further advances. To provide a challenging target for further progress on a practically important hardware-development task, we introduce CPU-Eval, a benchmark of 339 HDL-generation problems constructed from six CPUs. Drawn from practical CPU designs, including families fabricated in silicon, the problems span CPUs from small embedded cores to Linux-capable out-of-order cores and cover diverse CPU functions written in SystemVerilog, Chisel, and SpinalHDL. In each problem, an LLM performs the real CPU-development task of generating HDL. Across seven state-of-the-art LLMs, mean pass@1 is 45.14 percentage points lower on CPU-Eval than on VerilogEval v2 Spec-to-RTL, exposing capability differences obscured by VerilogEval's high pass rates. CPU-Eval reveals that pass@1 is lower for submodules with more source-code lines, which motivates fine-grained modular design for LLM-aided hardware generation. We also show that pass@1 is lower for CPUs written in less widely used HDLs, motivating designers to verify that an LLM is sufficiently proficient at generating code in the HDL they use before deployment.

papers.title: DELTA: Diagnosing Exploration Lineages via Twin-path Alignment - What Can Contrasting Design Paths Reveal About Microarchitectural Behavior?
papers.abstract: Architects have two mature instruments for performance work. Top-Down analysis tells them where a design loses its pipeline slots, and design-space exploration (DSE) tells them which configuration scores best. Neither explains why a search stops improving: why a backend-bound design rejects a prefetcher that the bottleneck label recommends, or why a capacity increase that helped in one configuration hurts in the next. This paper argues that the evidence needed to answer such questions is already produced during exploration and then discarded. Every parent-child edge in an exploration tree is a controlled intervention: one knob changes, the rest of the design is held fixed, and a cycle-level simulator measures the outcome. When the same edit helps under one parent and hurts under another, aligning the two parents localizes the interaction that decides its sign. We present DELTA, a simulator-grounded root-cause analysis tool that builds a Design Memory of such interventions during exploration and lets an architect query it afterwards. Each record stores the full parent configuration, the single applied edit, the measured and predicted IPC, a Top-Down breakdown from StallLens, our gem5 implementation of Top-Down, and its lineage. Unlike evolutionary LLM search, which keeps only high-scoring programs, DELTA keeps failed edges as evidence. The same memory also makes exploration efficient: on four SPEC CPU2017 workloads, the full system raises IPC by 55.5% in 22 simulated designs for $1.56 of model cost, predicts the IPC of its own proposals to within 3.3%, and keeps improving after a bottleneck-guided search stalls. A root-cause query over the recorded history led us to a usefulness-throttled variant of the Best-Offset prefetcher that improves IPC by 1.37% over the original in matched configurations.

papers.title: Verifiable Logical-Physical Contracts for Refactored On-Die Power Control Circuitry
papers.abstract: Recent literature allows independent hardware experiments to occupy a single die for scalable and cost-efficient silicon prototyping. Within this framework, specialized hardware functions including low-power control mechanisms can be offered as reusable on-die microservices. However, this requires well-defined contracts connecting digital requests to physical behavior. We present a checkable logical-physical contract formulation including a physical contract model describing service completion between client and provider through formally verified digital guarantees and physically validated completion conditions. We introduce Lightswitch, a proof-of-concept on-die power control microservice. We assess post-layout designs in TSMC 28nm and demonstrate how checkable contracts provide formal guarantees.

papers.title: Scaling Architectural Simulation to Giga Instructions Per Second
papers.abstract: The cost of detailed architectural simulation constrains design-space exploration, while parallelization across simulated cores offers limited host concurrency for single-core and small multicore targets. We present GIPSim, an instruction-driven simulator that derives instruction timing from dependencies and resource constraints, reducing the overhead of updating pipeline state every simulated cycle. It applies synchronization-guided temporal decomposition to recorded execution, exposing host parallelism beyond the target core count. GIPSim replays the resulting segments in parallel and aggregates their durations through a dependency graph to estimate overall execution time, with replay contexts reconstructed using retained microarchitectural state, warmup, and synchronization-guided cache eviction. This accounts for synchronization waits without requiring host workers to follow target execution order. We evaluate GIPSim using QEMU traces of application and operating system execution on multi-core x86-64, AArch64, and RV64GC systems. GIPSim achieves an average single-node simulation throughput of 13.8 million instructions per second (MIPS) with one worker and 1{,}010 MIPS with 96 workers, peaking at 1{,}421 MIPS. The corresponding mean absolute percentage errors in execution cycles relative to gem5 are 7.52\% and 7.43\%, respectively.

papers.title: On the Design of a Slow Control Interlock System for the European GateMate FPGA
papers.abstract: Slow Control Systems (SCSs) are essential for the monitoring, configuration, and protection of distributed safety-critical systems in scientific, industrial, and medical applications. Although software-based SCS architectures offer flexibility and scalability, they suffer from software aging and non-deterministic latencies, which limit long-term reliability and timely reaction to critical errors, often requiring additional hardware interlock systems. This paper presents an FPGA-centric lightweight Slow Control Interlock System (SCIS) designed to achieve deterministic ultra-low-latency reaction times in long-running dependable systems. System parameters are acquired and fused at runtime in a Supervisory Monitor Unit (SMU), enabling real-time fault condition classification and prioritization through configurable priority rules and triggering kill-switch actions with microsecond-scale latency. The proposed SMU has been described in VHDL as vendor-agnostic architecture, and assessed on the 28-nm GateMate M1A1 FPGA, using the open-source OSS-CAD-Suite toolchain. Experimental results show that the SMU architecture utilizes only 37,6% of LUTs, 9,4% of FFs, and 35,9% of BRAM. Furthermore, this low resource utilization allow to achieve 40,48 ms reconfiguration time, using OSS-CAD-Suite including gmpack v1.13. This is a key metric for rejuvenation and consequently for enabling aging mitigation in critical applications. Offloading the Ethernet stack to the W5500 Ethernet module and integrating the Grafana dashboard provides a lightweight, deterministic SCIS. This demonstrates the feasibility of our FPGA-centric architecture as a solution to the problem of combining ultra-low-latency interlock capabilities with the scalability of software-based systems.

papers.title: MOSAIC: Memory-Organized Search with Anti-Imitation Crossover for Training-Free Microarchitecture Optimization
papers.abstract: Large language models can generate cache-replacement policies. The central challenge is to retain performance on workloads excluded from the search. In our adaptations of published search methods, generated code resembles established policies, with cosine similarities of 0.78-0.84. The wider comparison also shows held-out harmonic-mean instructions-per-cycle (IPC) losses of 1.0-2.4%. We present MOSAIC, a search controller that improves policies without updating language-model weights. It stores concise lessons from previous evaluations rather than repeatedly copying high-scoring code. When improvement stops, it selects two high-scoring policies whose code embeddings differ and asks the model to combine their mechanisms. Novelty prompts and model rotation support this search; controlled memory edits test how the stored lessons affect later proposals. We evaluate cache replacement using intervention-level cross-validation and a wider comparison on ten memory-intensive SPEC2006 workloads. MOSAIC reaches a 51.1% peak hit rate on the primary search workload and a 47.9% held-out mean in the intervention study. Removing crossover reduces these values by 7.8 and 21.8 percentage points, respectively, whereas the tested stronger model improves the held-out mean by 0.4 points. In the wider IPC comparison, MOSAIC has the smallest held-out gap (0.31%) and the highest held-out IPC among the evaluated LLM configurations. Adapting the same controller to data prefetching gives a 4.8% mean speedup over the LRU reference configuration. The accompanying corpus contains 10,687 generated policies with lineage and per-iteration prompt logs.

papers.title: A Systematic Method of GPU Verification on Subsystem Modelling
papers.abstract: ARM Fast Model is a software modelling system for simulating multiple systems IPs integrated in a subsystem. Fast Model allows customer to run whole software stack as early as system IPs' specification is just ready. In this paper, we talk about a systematic method to enable GPU modelling and make whole system software stacks executable for both CPU and GPU in the integrated modelling environment, and eventually the major GPU IP can be verified. With our solution, we can directly run commercial benchmarks like Antutu and GFX Bench in Android target system with underlying ARM Fast Model mobile subsystem support. This was unbelievable in the past due to 3D rendering simulation for GPU verification is very slow. We also introduce some special techniques to improve performance. Eventually the whole software stack can directly work on real hardware without any changes as soon as the first tape-out is ready.

papers.title: ChiProgramBench: Can LLM Agents Rebuild Efficient Circuits from Pin-Level Experiments?
papers.abstract: Understanding a system that can be run but not inspected is a core engineering skill: one designs experiments, forms hypotheses about hidden state and timing, discards those that observations refute, and finally builds a replacement that works and is efficient. To evaluate this capability of LLM agents in the hardware domain, we present ChiProgramBench, 18 tasks derived from open-source processors, accelerators, codecs, transforms, interconnects, and control circuits. Agents can only drive and read the pins of a hidden, stateful simulated reference, then submit a gate-level netlist made of public library cells. Agents work in two settings: black-box discovery gives only anonymized functional pins and the interfaces of fixed memories, while function-guided reconstruction adds the circuit's purpose and each pin's role. Hidden test cases compare outputs with the reference cycle by cycle; power, delay, and area earn credit relative to the reference only when every case passes. Across 432 trials of 6 LLM agent configurations, successful agents recover algorithms and numerical conventions, yet only 12.0% of black-box and 14.8% of function-guided trials pass every case. Function-guided reconstruction raises the mean functional score, the cycle-weighted share of passed cases, from 24.6% to 30.9%. Of the 58 fully passing designs, only three improve on the reference's combined power, area, and delay, so behavioral recovery and efficient implementation remain distinct challenges.
